question: In 2021, Petrurgiya Plc adopted an investment plan for a ‘Facility for the production of stone wool and an energy plant to meet production needs’ in the village of Varbovka in the municipality of Pavlinki. Of particular concern to local communities is the ‘energy plant’ – i.e. waste incineration unit – which will burn incoming waste and thus pose a significant health and environmental risk.
The scale of the operation is huge – 1 160 tonnes of refuse-derived fuel (RDF) per day, 423 400 tonnes per year, and a total of 44 MW power output.

Directive 2011/92/EU on the assessment of the effects on the environment indicates, in the absence of a Best Available Techniques (BAT) reference document (BREF) for stone wool production, two BAT technologies for gas cleaning under BAT Conclusion 2012/134/EU for glass production – the fabric filter and wet electrostatic precipitator.

The strict regulation of technologies under BAT Conclusion 2019/2010 on waste incineration has been ignored. The production of stone wool is being used to mask the generation of electricity through the incineration of RDF. I would like to ask: 1.
Whether it is permissible to carry out waste incineration operations which do not conform to BAT Conclusion 2019/2010?

What monitoring the Commission is performing to prevent the circumvention of the Industrial Emissions Directive through the use of the BAT for industries other than the one actually involved in the production activities?
answer: To operate, the plants carrying out activities in the scope of Annex I (1) of the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED) (2) must hold a permit granted in compliance with the IED and the relevant Best Available Techniques (BAT) conclusions (3).

In the case highlighted by the Honourable Member, both BAT conclusions for waste incineration as well as for manufacturing of glass may be relevant as mandatory references for competent authorities when setting permit conditions. Competent authorities shall proactively identify the main activity of the installation at stake.
In complex cases, the competent authority should take due account of the following when deciding to proceed with permit issuance or reconsideration: —
The main purpose(s) of, and the product(s) produced by, the activities carried out at the installation;
The environmental impacts of the activities carried out at the installation;

The pursuance of the IED objectives and the general principles governing the basic obligations of the operator, including the avoidance of significant pollution, as laid down in Article 11 of the IED;
The scope and content of each BAT conclusions.

Based on the above, the competent authority may conclude that not only one, but several sets of BAT conclusions relate to the main activities of a given installation. The Commission does not carry out a systematic legal review of the permits at the level of each installation but aims at identifying persistent and structural breaches of EU legislation. |(⸱1|)∙ |(⸱2|)∙ |(⸱3|)∙

For waste incineration plant — point 5.2 letter a) and b) of the IED Annex I; for glass manufacture plants point 3.3 and 3.4 of the same Annex. Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 November 2010 on industrial emissions (integrated pollution prevention and control) ,OJ L 334, 17.12.2010, p. 17-119.

Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2019/2010 of 12 November 2019 establishing the best available techniques (BAT) conclusions, under Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council, for waste incineration, OJ L 312, 3.12.2019.

Commission Implementing Decision of 28 February 2012 establishing the best available techniques (BAT) conclusions under Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on industrial emissions for the manufacture of glass,OJ L 70, 8.3.2012, p. 1-62.
The Commission invites the Honourable Member to liaise with the relevant competent authoritie s (4), which are primarily responsible for assessing compliance of installations with EU legislation.
